newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile toughens anti-smog measures in capital.
newsitem.headline: Chile toughens anti-smog measures in capital.

text.p: Chilean President Eduardo Frei announced tough new restrictions on cars and factories on Friday in smog-choked Santiago, which is suffering its worst pollution crisis in years.

The government will declare an "environmental alert" whenever smog levels in the capital, one of the world's worst- polluted cities, rise above 200 on an official air quality scale, Frei said in a speech at the Moneda Presidential Palace.
"Each time this occurs ... there will be a public announcement of the alert so that the public can take all precautionary measures," he said.

Frei unveiled his plan shortly after authorities declared a state of "pre-emergency" in the city for an unprecedented four days in a row. Pre-emergency measures, which include controls on vehicles and industry, are imposed when smog levels hit 300.
Public alarm over air pollution has grown in recent days, with television showing state hospitals packed with children and old people being treated for respiratory problems.
A hazy gray cloud usually blankets the city for much of the Southern Hemisphere winter, but the situation has been made worse than usual this year by a lack of rain in recent weeks to clear the air.
Because Santiago lies in a valley surrounded by towering Andean peaks and coastal mountains, there is virtually no wind to sweep the contamination away.

Steps to help the city's residents breathe easier include stricter restrictions on cars, trucks and buses that will keep an extra 250,000 vehicles off city streets when pollution is serious, Frei said.
Other measures include a reduction in parking in the streets, a restriction on the movement of trucks in the city centre and cuts in emissions from factories.
The plan, the second to tackle pollution in the city this decade, will cost at least $600 million, of which 40 percent will come from the state.
One of its main goals is to reduce the number of premature deaths caused by the smog, which doctors say weakens the body's immune system and increases the risk of lung cancer.
If programme targets are met, by 2011 more than 10,000 premature deaths caused by particulate matter and more than 500 caused by ozone will be avoided, officials say.
They blame much of the pollution on a sharp rise in car ownership, uncontrolled expansion of the city and a lack of control over factory emissions.

A recent World Bank survey showed Santiago to be the world's sixth-most-polluted city in terms of particle levels, better than Calcutta or Mexico City but worse than Brazil's industrial capital of Sao Paulo.
